nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: How many worldviews are summarized in the text?
nodes.answer: Four worldviews are summarized in the text.
nodes.paragraph: Each worldview represents a coherent package of pat- terns of social relations and cultural biases. Cultural biases are shared fundamental values (equality, freedom, order, and good/bad luck) and beliefs (underlying problem definitions, positions, strategies, and preferred policy instruments) about human and physical nature related to the four types of social relations (Newman et al., 2018; Oli & Swedlow, 2022; Sotirov & Winkel, 2016). Social relations refer to two dimensions: a preference for low or high external rules on human behavior called grid (thus more or less individual free- dom or constraints) and a preference for low or high group , referring to people S prefer - ence of how to organize their interactions with people (ranging from individual choices to collective decisions). The worldviews with their cultural biases and corresponding social relations and their reciprocal reinforcement are hence conceptualized through a grid-group typology (Thompson et al., 1990; see also Sotirov & Winkel, 2016, Swedlow, 2012). The four worldviews are summarized in Fig. 1. Each quadrant along the two axes of high/low group and grid represents one worldview.

nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What outcome is associated with exposure to new experiences and perspectives in transformative learning?
nodes.answer: Exposure to new experiences and perspectives in transformative learning can result in changes in frames of reference, shifts in beliefs, and a motivation to act.
nodes.paragraph: Mezirow characterizes learning as a process of critical self-reflection, leading to re-evaluating one S perspective to foster a more comprehensive, discerning, and interactive understanding of personal experiences ( 1991 , p. xvi). The process is a form of metacognitive reasoning, which is specifically adult-oriented and can ultimately pave the way for acquiring knowledge and deeper comprehension. Such reasoning can alter a person S frame of reference (i.e., their cognitive framework) and may open opportunities for transforming beliefs, emancipation, and societal change through individual action (Mezirow, 2003 ). According to Mezirow ( 1991 ), learning is transformative when it changes behaviour or a new form of action. This type of learning involves a change in a person S cognitive frame of reference. It typically begins with a disorienting event, which may be either dramatic (epochal) or gradual (incremental) (Mezirow, 2003 ). In essence, transformative learning illustrates how exposure to new experiences and perspectives can result in changes in frames of reference, shifts in beliefs, and a motivation to act upon newfound understandings, collectively fostering pathways to social and structural change (Mezirow, 1991 , 1997 , 2003 ).
